title: Muscle Energy Systems & Fuel Use
summary: Understand how skeletal muscle makes ATP and selects fuels across different intensities and durations.

lessons.title: The Phosphocreatine System and Immediate Energy

levels.kid:
Your muscles run on a tiny energy coin called **ATP**. Every time a muscle squeezes, it spends ATP. But here is the funny part: your muscles only keep a few seconds' worth of coins in their pocket!

So muscles carry a backup piggy bank called **phosphocreatine**. When the ATP coins run low, phosphocreatine quickly hands over a piece to turn a spent coin back into a fresh one. It is super fast, like a sprinter.

That is why you can jump, throw or sprint hard right away. But the piggy bank is small. After about ten seconds of all-out effort, it is mostly empty. Then you rest, and in a few minutes your muscles fill it up again.
levels.hs:
Muscles contract using **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate). When ATP is split into **ADP** (adenosine diphosphate) and phosphate, energy is released that powers the myosin heads pulling on actin. The problem: a muscle stores only enough ATP for roughly 2 seconds of maximal effort.

The first backup is the **phosphocreatine (PCr) system**, also called the **ATP-PCr** or **phosphagen system**. Phosphocreatine is a molecule that stores a high-energy phosphate. The enzyme **creatine kinase** moves that phosphate onto ADP, rebuilding ATP almost instantly:

- PCr + ADP → creatine + ATP

Key features:
- It needs no oxygen, so it is **anaerobic**.
- It works in a single step, so it delivers ATP faster than any other system.
- Its store is small, lasting about **10 seconds** of all-out work.

Real example: a 100 m sprinter leaves the blocks powered largely by ATP and PCr. By the last part of the race, PCr is heavily depleted and top speed falls slightly, which is why even world-class sprinters decelerate near the finish.

After exercise, PCr is rebuilt using ATP made with oxygen in the mitochondria. About half is restored in roughly 30 seconds, and nearly all within 3 to 5 minutes. That is why weightlifters rest several minutes between heavy sets.
levels.college:
The **phosphagen system** buffers ATP during sudden increases in demand. Resting muscle contains roughly 20-25 mmol of ATP per kg dry weight, but about 3 to 4 times more **phosphocreatine (PCr)**. During maximal contraction ATP turnover can rise more than 100-fold over rest, so PCr is consumed within seconds while ATP concentration falls surprisingly little.

**The creatine kinase reaction**
- PCr + ADP + H+ ⇌ creatine + ATP
- Catalyzed by **creatine kinase (CK)**; near equilibrium, so it responds instantly to rising ADP.
- It *consumes* a proton, so PCr breakdown slightly alkalinizes the muscle early in exercise.
- Maximal ATP resynthesis rate from PCr is the highest of any pathway (several mmol ATP per kg dry muscle per second), but capacity is small.

**Adenylate kinase (myokinase)** offers a second immediate route: 2 ADP → ATP + AMP. The rising AMP activates phosphofructokinase and glycogen phosphorylase, signaling glycolysis to speed up. AMP is then deaminated to IMP and ammonia by AMP deaminase.

**Time course in all-out work**
- PCr contributes most of the ATP in the first ~6 seconds.
- It is heavily depleted by ~10-15 seconds; glycolysis increasingly takes over.
- No system ever works in isolation: glycolysis is already active within the first seconds.

**Recovery**
PCr resynthesis relies on **oxidative phosphorylation**, so it is an aerobic process. Recovery is roughly exponential, with a half-time of about 30 seconds in healthy muscle. Recovery is slower when blood flow or oxygen delivery is reduced.

**Fiber differences**
Type II (fast) fibers have higher PCr stores and faster PCr breakdown during sprints. Type I fibers recover PCr faster because of their greater mitochondrial content.

**Creatine** is synthesized in the kidney and liver from arginine, glycine and methionine and taken up into muscle by the transporter **SLC6A8**. Its breakdown product, **creatinine**, is excreted by the kidney.
levels.phd:
The phosphagen system is best viewed as both an energy buffer and a spatial energy shuttle. Because creatine kinase (CK) operates near equilibrium, the ratio [PCr]/[Cr] tracks [ATP]/[ADP][H+], holding cytosolic ATP nearly constant while free ADP rises. Free ADP, which is micromolar and not directly measurable, is calculated from the CK equilibrium and is a key regulator of mitochondrial respiration.

**Isoforms and the PCr shuttle.** CK exists as cytosolic dimers (MM in muscle, BB in brain, MB in heart) and as octameric mitochondrial isoforms (sarcomeric **sMtCK** in muscle) located in the intermembrane space. Bessman and Wallimann's **phosphocreatine circuit** hypothesis proposes that sMtCK, coupled to the adenine nucleotide translocase, converts newly exported ATP into PCr. PCr, a smaller and more diffusible molecule than ATP, then carries the energy to myofibrillar MM-CK and to CK bound to SERCA and Na+/K+-ATPase, where ATP is regenerated locally.

**Measurement.** Classic needle biopsy studies (Hultman, Bergström) quantified PCr depletion. **31P magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS)** now noninvasively tracks PCr, Pi and pH. The chemical shift between Pi and PCr gives intracellular pH. The PCr recovery time constant (τPCr, typically ~30-50 s in healthy quadriceps) is an index of in vivo oxidative capacity.

**Quantitative contribution.** Studies of 30-s maximal cycling (Gaitanos, Bogdanis) show that in repeated sprints, glycolytic ATP falls sharply across bouts while PCr provides a growing share. Sprint performance correlates with PCr resynthesis, so aerobic fitness supports repeated-sprint ability.

**Fatigue nuance.** PCr hydrolysis raises inorganic phosphate (Pi). Accumulating Pi, rather than lactate or H+ alone, is now considered a major cause of early fatigue. It impairs cross-bridge force and can precipitate with calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reducing calcium release.

**Knockouts.** CK-deficient mice survive with surprisingly modest phenotypes, such as impaired burst activity and altered calcium handling. This suggests extensive compensation, mainly through adenylate kinase and glycolysis. It also challenges strict versions of the shuttle model, which remain debated.
levels.expert:
For clinician-scientists, the phosphagen axis surfaces in diagnostics, disease and supplementation.

**Creatine kinase as a biomarker.** Serum CK reflects sarcolemmal leakage. Pitfalls include large rises after unaccustomed eccentric exercise, which can reach thousands of U/L in healthy people and peak about 3-5 days later. Ethnicity and muscle mass also shift reference ranges. Exertional rhabdomyolysis, statin myopathy, inflammatory myopathies and muscular dystrophies elevate CK. Interpret CK alongside myoglobinuria, kidney function and potassium, because the danger is acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia, not the CK number itself. CK-MB has largely been superseded by troponin for myocardial infarction.

**Creatine deficiency syndromes.** These are three inborn errors:
- **AGAT** and **GAMT** deficiency, which affect synthesis.
- **SLC6A8** transporter deficiency, which is X-linked.

They present with intellectual disability, speech delay, seizures and movement disorders, underscoring the brain's dependence on PCr. Brain proton MRS shows an absent creatine peak. Synthesis defects respond partly to creatine supplementation; the transporter defect largely does not, because creatine cannot enter neurons. This is an active therapeutic research area.

**Supplementation.** Creatine monohydrate is one of the best-evidenced ergogenic aids. It raises muscle total creatine and PCr by roughly 10-30%, depending on baseline. This improves repeated high-intensity efforts and training volume. Vegetarians and low responders differ in response. Water retention causes early weight gain. Serum creatinine rises without true loss of kidney function, so a misread estimated GFR is a real clinical pitfall. Cystatin C can clarify this. Trials in ALS, Huntington's and Parkinson's disease were negative. Studies in depression, ageing sarcopenia and traumatic brain injury continue.

**Neurosurgical angle.** Cerebral PCr and BB-CK buffer neurons during ischemia; PCr falls within seconds of energy failure, before ATP collapses. 31P-MRS of muscle is used in mitochondrial myopathy workups, where prolonged τPCr signals impaired oxidative phosphorylation.

**Open questions.** Is PCr's energy-shuttle role essential or redundant? Can brain creatine be raised meaningfully? Are cyclocreatine and related analogs viable for transporter deficiency?

keyPoints: Muscle stores only ~2 s of ATP; phosphocreatine is the immediate backup
Creatine kinase transfers phosphate from PCr to ADP to rebuild ATP
The phosphagen system is anaerobic, fastest, but lasts ~10 s all-out
PCr resynthesis is aerobic, half-time ~30 s, near-complete in 3-5 min
PCr breakdown consumes H+ and releases Pi, a key fatigue factor
Serum CK, creatinine and creatine deficiency syndromes link it to the clinic

test.q: Which enzyme transfers phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP?
test.explain: Creatine kinase catalyzes PCr + ADP → creatine + ATP. Phosphofructokinase is a glycolytic enzyme.

test.q: How long does the phosphagen system roughly sustain all-out effort?
test.explain: PCr stores are heavily depleted after about 10 seconds of maximal work.

test.q: Why is the PCr system the fastest source of ATP?
choices: It uses oxygen delivered by blood
It regenerates ATP in a single step
test.explain: One enzymatic step gives the highest rate of ATP resynthesis, though capacity is small.

test.q: What process rebuilds phosphocreatine after exercise?
test.explain: PCr resynthesis relies on ATP from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, so recovery is aerobic.

test.q: About how long does it take to restore half of depleted PCr?
test.explain: Recovery is roughly exponential with a half-time near 30 seconds and is near-complete in 3-5 minutes.

test.q: Early in intense exercise, PCr breakdown tends to make muscle:
test.explain: The creatine kinase reaction consumes a proton, which alkalinizes the muscle slightly.

test.q: Why do weightlifters rest several minutes between heavy sets?
choices: To clear fat from muscle fibers
test.explain: PCr takes about 3-5 minutes to recover nearly fully, supporting the next maximal effort.

test.q: The adenylate kinase reaction converts two ADP into:
test.explain: 2 ADP → ATP + AMP. Rising AMP also stimulates glycolysis.

test.q: Which fibers recover PCr fastest after exercise?
test.explain: Type I fibers have more mitochondria, so they resynthesize PCr faster. Type II fibers store more PCr.

test.q: Because it needs no oxygen, the phosphagen system is described as ___.
test.explain: It runs without oxygen, although its recovery depends on aerobic metabolism.

test.q: What breakdown product of creatine is excreted by the kidney?
test.explain: Creatinine is the waste product used to estimate kidney function.

test.q: Creatine enters muscle cells through the transporter called SLC6___.
test.explain: SLC6A8 is the creatine transporter in muscle and brain.

kidTest.q: What is the energy coin muscles spend?
kidTest.explain: Muscles use ATP for energy every time they squeeze.

kidTest.q: How long does the backup piggy bank last when you go all-out?
kidTest.explain: Phosphocreatine runs low after about ten seconds of hard effort.

kidTest.q: Which activity uses this fast energy most?
kidTest.explain: Quick, powerful moves like sprinting use the fast backup.

kidTest.q: How does the piggy bank fill up again?
kidTest.explain: Rest lets muscles rebuild phosphocreatine in a few minutes.

kidTest.q: The backup piggy bank is called phospho _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Phosphocreatine quickly turns spent coins back into fresh ATP.

advancedTest.q: During a maximal sprint, ATP concentration falls little while PCr drops sharply. The best explanation is:
choices: Creatine kinase sits near equilibrium and buffers ATP
Glycolysis supplies most of the ATP in the first seconds
Adenylate kinase strongly inhibits ATP hydrolysis
advancedTest.explain: Near-equilibrium CK uses PCr to regenerate ATP as ADP rises, so PCr falls in place of ATP. Glycolysis is active early, but PCr supplies most ATP in the first seconds.

advancedTest.q: A patient with mitochondrial myopathy has a prolonged 31P-MRS PCr recovery time constant. This mainly reflects:
choices: Excess creatine kinase leaking into serum
advancedTest.explain: PCr resynthesis depends on oxidative phosphorylation, so slowed τPCr indexes impaired mitochondrial capacity.

advancedTest.q: Across repeated 30-s sprints, why does aerobic fitness predict performance?
choices: It increases glycolytic ATP in later bouts
It speeds PCr resynthesis between bouts
advancedTest.explain: Glycolytic contribution falls across bouts while PCr's share grows, and PCr recovery is oxidative.

advancedTest.q: Why does creatine supplementation help synthesis defects more than SLC6A8 deficiency?
choices: Supplements are converted to creatinine first
Synthesis defects lack creatine kinase enzyme
Transporter loss stops creatine entering neurons
advancedTest.explain: In AGAT/GAMT deficiency, dietary creatine can enter cells; without SLC6A8, uptake into brain cells fails.

lessons.title: Glycolysis, Lactate and the Lactate Shuttle

levels.kid:
Your muscles run on a tiny energy coin called **ATP**. When you sprint, they need lots of coins, fast.

One quick way to make coins is to snap sugar in half. This is called **glycolysis**. It is fast, like a microwave, but it makes only a few coins each time.

Snapping sugar leaves behind a leftover called **lactate**. People used to think lactate was trash that made muscles burn and get sore. Scientists now know that is mostly wrong!

Lactate is more like a packed lunch. Your muscles, heart and brain can pick it up and use it for more energy. Lactate gets passed around the body, like friends sharing snacks at school.
levels.hs:
Muscles need **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) to contract. **Glycolysis** is the pathway that breaks one glucose molecule (6 carbons) into two **pyruvate** molecules (3 carbons each) in the cytoplasm. It needs no oxygen and gives a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose, or 3 ATP if it starts from stored **glycogen**.

Glycolysis is fast but needs a helper molecule, **NAD+**, which gets used up as it becomes NADH. To keep glycolysis running, the enzyme **lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** turns pyruvate into **lactate**, which regenerates NAD+.

Big myths to drop:
- Lactate is made even when there is plenty of oxygen, especially when glycolysis runs fast.
- Lactate is not "lactic acid" waste. At body pH it exists as lactate, and the acidity comes mainly from ATP breakdown and other reactions.
- Lactate does not cause next-day soreness. That comes from small muscle damage and inflammation.

The **lactate shuttle**, proposed by physiologist George Brooks in the 1980s, says lactate is a fuel that moves between cells. For example, during a hard 800 m run, fast-twitch fibers make lactate. Nearby slow-twitch fibers and the heart take it up and burn it for energy. The liver can also turn it back into glucose. This recycling is called the **Cori cycle**.
levels.college:
**Glycolysis** is the 10-step cytosolic conversion of glucose to 2 pyruvate. The investment phase uses 2 ATP. The payoff phase yields 4 ATP plus 2 NADH, for a net of 2 ATP. Starting from glycogen, **glycogen phosphorylase** releases glucose-1-phosphate and skips the hexokinase step, so the net is 3 ATP.

Key control points:
- **Hexokinase**, inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate.
- **Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)**, the main rate-limiting enzyme. AMP, ADP and Pi activate it; ATP, citrate and low pH inhibit it.
- **Glycogen phosphorylase**, activated by Ca2+ (contraction), AMP and epinephrine via cAMP/PKA.
- **Pyruvate kinase**, activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (feed-forward).

**Why lactate forms.** Glycolysis consumes NAD+ at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Pyruvate has two fates: entry into mitochondria through pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), or reduction by **LDH** to lactate, which regenerates NAD+. LDH is fast and the reaction strongly favors lactate. So lactate rises whenever glycolytic flux outpaces mitochondrial pyruvate uptake. This happens during high intensity, fast-fiber recruitment and adrenaline surges, even when the muscle has plenty of oxygen.

**Acidosis.** Each lactate leaves with a proton through monocarboxylate transporters, but H+ comes mainly from ATP hydrolysis. Lactate production actually consumes a proton.

**The lactate shuttle.**
- **Cell-to-cell**: lactate moves out through **MCT4** (glycolytic fibers) and into cells through **MCT1** (oxidative fibers and heart).
- **Organ level**: the heart, liver and brain take up blood lactate. The liver and kidney use it for gluconeogenesis (the **Cori cycle**).
- During exercise, most lactate is oxidized, not converted back to glucose.

**Lactate threshold**: the intensity at which blood lactate begins to rise sharply. This happens when appearance exceeds clearance. It predicts endurance performance better than VO2max among trained athletes.
levels.phd:
Classical theory held that lactate signals O2 deficit. Hill and Meyerhof's lactic acid model of the 1920s, and Wasserman's "anaerobic threshold", framed it as dysoxic waste. Two lines of evidence overturned this. First, Connett and colleagues used myoglobin saturation in dog gracilis muscle and found that intracellular PO2 stayed above the critical mitochondrial PO2 even while lactate was released. Richardson's later proton MRS work in humans showed the same thing. Second, isotope tracer studies by Brooks showed that lactate turnover rises dramatically in exercise, and most of the label is oxidized.

The mass-action logic is decisive. LDH's equilibrium constant favors lactate, and cytosolic LDH activity exceeds PDH capacity by orders of magnitude. Lactate/pyruvate ratios are therefore typically about 10 or higher at rest, rising sharply with flux. Lactate is the obligatory product of fast glycolysis, set by the gap between flux and PDH activity. PDH is activated by Ca2+ (via PDH phosphatase) and by pyruvate (via inhibition of PDK), and inhibited by acetyl-CoA, NADH and PDK4.

**Transport.** MCTs (SLC16 family) are proton-linked symporters that need the chaperone basigin (CD147). MCT1 has a high affinity (Km about 3.5-10 mM) and dominates in oxidative fibers. MCT4 has a low affinity (Km about 25-30 mM) and suits efflux; it is HIF-1α inducible. Endurance training upregulates MCT1, increasing clearance and shifting the lactate curve rightward.

**Intracellular shuttle.** Brooks proposed a mitochondrial lactate oxidation complex made of MCT1, CD147, mitochondrial LDH and cytochrome oxidase. This remains debated. Sahlin and others found negligible direct lactate oxidation in isolated mitochondria and argued that cytosolic conversion to pyruvate explains the data.

**Acid-base.** Robergs argued that glycolysis plus ATP hydrolysis releases H+, while LDH consumes it, so 'lactic acidosis' is a misnomer. Stewart's strong-ion approach treats lactate as a strong anion that lowers the strong ion difference. The two frameworks emphasize different causality, and it remains a semantic and quantitative controversy.

**Astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle.** Pellerin and Magistretti (1994) proposed glutamate-stimulated astrocytic glycolysis that supplies neurons with lactate. Exercise raises brain lactate uptake, supporting a muscle-to-brain fuel route.
levels.expert:
Clinically, lactate is a marker of stress, not simply hypoxia. In sepsis, epinephrine acting on β2 receptors stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, which drives aerobic glycolysis. Hepatic clearance also falls. This explains why hyperlactatemia predicts mortality in Surviving Sepsis criteria (a level above 2 mmol/L with vasopressor need defines septic shock), yet does not prove tissue hypoxia. Clinicians distinguish type A (hypoperfusion) from type B lactic acidosis. Type B includes metformin toxicity through mitochondrial complex I and glycerophosphate dehydrogenase inhibition, linezolid, propofol infusion syndrome, thiamine deficiency (a PDH cofactor) and β2-agonist effects. In trauma and post-craniotomy patients, an isolated lactate rise during salbutamol or epinephrine infusion can be iatrogenic rather than a sign of occult shock.

Neurocritical care has adopted lactate as fuel. Cerebral microdialysis in traumatic brain injury reports the lactate/pyruvate ratio, where above 25-40 suggests metabolic crisis. A high ratio with low pyruvate implies ischemia, whereas a high ratio with normal pyruvate suggests mitochondrial dysfunction. Bouzier-Sore and Carteron's group have tested hypertonic lactate infusion in TBI. It spared glucose, lowered intracranial pressure and supplied neuronal fuel in small trials, but outcome evidence remains preliminary.

Lactate is also a signaling molecule, or "lactormone":
- It acts on the receptor **HCAR1 (GPR81)** to inhibit adipocyte lipolysis.
- It stabilizes HIF and induces PGC-1α and VEGF.
- Exercise lactate drives hippocampal BDNF via SIRT1 (El Hayek 2019).
- **Histone lactylation**, discovered by Zhang and Zhao (2019), links glycolytic flux to gene expression in macrophages and tumors.

In oncology, the Warburg effect is a pathological lactate shuttle. Glycolytic MCT4-expressing cells feed oxidative MCT1-expressing cells. The MCT1 inhibitor AZD3965 has entered early trials.

In sport testing, pitfalls abound. Lactate thresholds (LT1, LT2, OBLA at 4 mmol/L, Dmax) are protocol-dependent. Stage length, sampling site (earlobe vs fingertip), the analyzer and glycogen status all shift values. Low glycogen lowers lactate at a given workload and creates a false "improvement". Inherited MCT1 deficiency causes exercise-induced muscle injury. McArdle disease (myophosphorylase deficiency) produces a flat lactate response on forearm testing.

Open questions remain: the mitochondrial LDH controversy, how much lactate the brain really oxidizes during exercise, and the causal role of lactylation.

keyPoints: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate, netting 2 ATP (3 from glycogen) without oxygen
LDH converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running
Lactate forms whenever glycolytic flux outpaces mitochondrial uptake, even with plenty of oxygen
Lactate is a fuel, not waste, and does not cause next-day soreness
The lactate shuttle moves lactate via MCT4 out and MCT1 in to heart, oxidative fibers and liver
The lactate threshold marks where blood lactate appearance exceeds clearance

test.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis starting from one blood glucose molecule?
test.explain: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP and produces 4, for a net of 2. Starting from glycogen gives 3 because the hexokinase step is skipped.

test.q: Why does muscle convert pyruvate to lactate?
choices: To store extra oxygen in muscle
test.explain: LDH turns NADH back into NAD+, which glycolysis needs at the GAPDH step.

test.q: Which enzyme is the main rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
test.explain: PFK-1 is the key control point. AMP and ADP activate it, while ATP, citrate and low pH inhibit it.

test.q: According to modern evidence, lactate rises during hard exercise mainly because:
choices: The liver releases its stored lactate into blood
Working muscle fibers run short of oxygen
Red blood cells produce extra lactate in exercise
test.explain: Muscle oxygen stays adequate. Lactate rises because fast glycolysis exceeds PDH and mitochondrial capacity.

test.q: What mainly causes muscle soreness a day or two after hard exercise?
test.explain: Delayed soreness comes from small muscle damage and inflammation. Lactate is cleared within about an hour.

test.q: Which transporter mainly carries lactate INTO oxidative fibers and heart muscle?
test.explain: MCT1 is high-affinity and suited to uptake. MCT4 mainly exports lactate from glycolytic fibers.

test.q: During exercise, most lactate produced is:
test.explain: Tracer studies show most lactate is oxidized by muscle and heart. A smaller share becomes glucose in the liver.

test.q: The lactate threshold is the intensity at which:
test.explain: Lactate is present even at rest. The threshold marks where appearance outpaces removal and blood levels climb sharply.

test.q: Who proposed the lactate shuttle hypothesis?
test.explain: Brooks proposed it in the 1980s. Hill, Meyerhof and Wasserman framed lactate as an oxygen-deficit product.

test.q: The liver recycling lactate back into glucose is called the ___ cycle.
test.explain: The Cori cycle carries lactate to the liver for gluconeogenesis and returns glucose to muscle.

test.q: Which enzyme (abbreviated LDH) converts pyruvate to lactate? Give its full name.
test.explain: Lactate dehydrogenase catalyzes pyruvate + NADH to lactate + NAD+.

test.q: Glycolysis splits glucose into two molecules of ___.
test.explain: Each 6-carbon glucose yields two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules.

kidTest.q: What is the energy coin muscles use?
kidTest.explain: ATP is the energy coin that powers muscles.

kidTest.q: What does glycolysis do to sugar?
kidTest.explain: Glycolysis splits sugar in half to make quick energy.

kidTest.q: How fast is glycolysis?
kidTest.explain: It is fast like a microwave, but makes few coins.

kidTest.q: What do scientists now think lactate is?
kidTest.explain: Lactate is like a packed lunch that the heart, muscles and brain can use.

kidTest.q: The leftover from snapping sugar is called l _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Lactate is the leftover, and the body shares it as fuel.

advancedTest.q: Connett's myoglobin measurements showed lactate efflux while intracellular PO2 stayed above critical levels. This most directly implies:
choices: Lactate is made mainly by red blood cells
Mitochondria fail at moderate exercise intensity
Lactate output reflects glycolytic flux, not dysoxia
Myoglobin itself produces lactate under strain
advancedTest.explain: If oxygen is adequate yet lactate is released, the cause is mass action from fast glycolysis outpacing PDH, not an oxygen shortage.

advancedTest.q: Endurance training shifts the blood lactate curve rightward. Which mechanism best explains this?
choices: Higher MCT4 expression in heart muscle
Greater MCT1 expression and lactate clearance
Loss of LDH activity in fast fibers
Reduced PFK-1 content in slow fibers
advancedTest.explain: Training upregulates MCT1 and oxidative capacity, so clearance rises and lactate accumulates at higher intensities.

advancedTest.q: A septic patient on epinephrine has rising lactate with normal perfusion markers. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Failure of red cell oxygen delivery
Occult tissue hypoxia in the gut
advancedTest.explain: β2 stimulation increases Na+/K+-ATPase demand and glycolytic flux, a type B rise that does not imply hypoxia.

advancedTest.q: Microdialysis in TBI shows a high lactate/pyruvate ratio with normal pyruvate. This suggests:
choices: Classic ischemia with low substrate supply
advancedTest.explain: High LPR with low pyruvate points to ischemia. With normal pyruvate, it points to impaired mitochondrial oxidation.

lessons.title: Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation in Muscle

levels.kid:
Your muscles have tiny power plants inside them called **mitochondria**. They are so small you need a strong microscope to see them.

These power plants take food (sugar and fat) and the oxygen you breathe in. They slowly burn them to make the energy coins your muscles spend, called **ATP**.

This way of making energy is slower than the quick bursts your muscles can do, but it makes LOTS of energy and can keep going for a long time. That's why you can walk, swim or ride a bike for ages.

When you breathe out, some of what leaves is carbon dioxide, a leftover from this burning. If you train a lot, your muscles build more power plants!
levels.hs:
Muscles run on **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate), but they store very little, enough for only a few seconds of hard work. For anything longer than a couple of minutes, most ATP comes from **oxidative phosphorylation** inside the **mitochondria**.

Here is the basic idea:
- Fuels (from glucose and fatty acids) are broken down into a molecule called **acetyl-CoA**.
- Acetyl-CoA enters the **Krebs cycle** (citric acid cycle), which strips off high-energy electrons and loads them onto carriers called **NADH** and **FADH2**. Carbon dioxide is released.
- These carriers deliver electrons to the **electron transport chain**, a series of proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
- As electrons pass down the chain, protons are pumped across the membrane, building up a gradient, like water behind a dam.
- **Oxygen** is the final electron catcher; it combines with protons to form water.
- Protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, a rotating molecular machine that makes ATP.

One glucose molecule fully oxidized yields roughly 30-32 ATP, far more than the 2 from glycolysis alone. The trade-off is speed: this system produces ATP more slowly than the phosphocreatine system or glycolysis.

Example: a marathon runner gets well over 95% of their energy aerobically, which is why endurance athletes train to increase the number of mitochondria in their muscles.
levels.college:
Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) couples substrate oxidation to ATP synthesis via the **chemiosmotic mechanism** (Mitchell, 1961).

**Feeding the chain.** Pyruvate enters the matrix via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier and is decarboxylated by **pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH)** to acetyl-CoA. Long-chain fatty acids enter via **carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-1)** and undergo beta-oxidation, generating acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH2. The TCA cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA to CO2, producing 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP per turn.

**The chain.**
- **Complex I** (NADH dehydrogenase) passes electrons to ubiquinone, pumping 4 H+.
- **Complex II** (succinate dehydrogenase) feeds FADH2-derived electrons in without pumping.
- **Complex III** (cytochrome bc1) pumps via the Q cycle, passing electrons to cytochrome c.
- **Complex IV** (cytochrome c oxidase) reduces O2 to water, pumping protons.
- **Complex V** (ATP synthase): about 2.7 H+ per ATP in mammals given the c8 rotor, plus 1 H+ for phosphate/ADP transport.

This gives P/O ratios near 2.5 (NADH) and 1.5 (FADH2), and roughly 32 ATP per glucose and ~106 per palmitate.

**Control.** ADP availability is the key regulator (**respiratory control**): when contraction hydrolyzes ATP, rising ADP and Pi drive ATP synthase and dissipate the gradient, accelerating electron flow. Calcium released during contraction also activates PDH and TCA dehydrogenases, providing feed-forward activation.

**Capacity.** Maximal ATP turnover by OXPHOS is roughly half that of glycolysis and far below phosphocreatine, so OXPHOS dominates in efforts lasting beyond about 2 minutes. Oxygen delivery, mitochondrial content and enzyme activity together set VO2max and sustainable power. Myoglobin buffers and facilitates intracellular O2 diffusion, and mitochondrial density in elite endurance athletes can be double that of untrained people.
levels.phd:
**Kinetic control of muscle respiration.** Chance and Williams (1955) defined respiratory control by ADP; in muscle, the creatine kinase **phosphocreatine shuttle** links myofibrillar ATPases to mitochondria. Mitochondrial creatine kinase (MtCK), coupled to the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) in the intermembrane space, means that creatine and PCr, rather than free ADP, carry much of the signal in oxidative fibers. Apparent Km for ADP is high in permeabilized slow-twitch fibers (~300 µM) but low in isolated mitochondria (~20 µM), revealing diffusion restriction via VDAC/tubulin interactions. Debate continues over whether control is mainly by [ADP], phosphorylation potential (ΔGATP), or parallel activation (Korzeniewski's each-step activation model) in which Ca2+ and other signals co-activate multiple complexes, explaining how VO2 can rise many-fold with modest changes in metabolite levels.

**Kinetics in vivo.** 31P-MRS shows PCr recovery after exercise follows monoexponential kinetics; the time constant (τPCr, ~30-50 s healthy) is a validated index of in vivo oxidative capacity. Pulmonary VO2 on-kinetics (phase II τ ~20-40 s) mirror muscle O2 consumption; the O2 deficit is covered by PCr and glycolysis. Above critical power, a **slow component** appears, attributed to progressive recruitment of less efficient fibers and fatigue-related efficiency loss.

**Supercomplexes and cristae.** Complexes I, III and IV assemble into respirasomes, their stability influenced by cardiolipin and the scaffolding factor SCAF1 (COX7A2L); their functional significance (channeling vs stability) is disputed. Cristae shape, governed by OPA1 and the MICOS complex, affects respiratory capacity per mitochondrion; training increases cristae density.

**Distribution.** Muscle mitochondria form a connected reticulum (Glancy et al., 2015) that conducts membrane potential from the periphery to the fiber interior, raising the possibility of a power grid with distributed proton motive force.

**Biogenesis.** Contraction signals (AMPK, CaMKII, p38 MAPK) converge on **PGC-1α**, coactivating NRF1/2 and TFAM. Yet PGC-1α knockout mice still adapt to training, showing redundancy.
levels.expert:
**Clinical measurement.** In the clinic, mitochondrial function in muscle is inferred from several tools, each with blind spots. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing reveals low peak VO2, an early ventilatory threshold, and an exaggerated cardiac output response relative to VO2 (a hyperkinetic circulation) in primary mitochondrial myopathy, because O2 extraction is impaired. 31P-MRS τPCr, high-resolution respirometry on biopsy samples (Oroboros), and near-infrared spectroscopy for muscle oxygen saturation complement it. A pitfall: low VO2max from deconditioning and from true OXPHOS defects can look similar. The low arteriovenous O2 difference with high venous O2 saturation points to a mitochondrial cause.

**Mitochondrial myopathies.** Mutations in mtDNA (e.g., MELAS m.3243A>G; single large deletions in chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia) or nuclear genes produce exercise intolerance, lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibers. Heteroplasmy and threshold effects explain variable phenotypes. Endurance training improves function, partly through shifting heteroplasmy and expanding mitochondrial mass; resistance training may promote satellite-cell-derived wild-type mtDNA (gene shifting), though evidence is limited.

**Pharmacology relevant to OXPHOS.**
- **Statins** lower coenzyme Q10 synthesis; their role in statin myopathy is debated, and CoQ10 supplementation trials are mostly negative.
- **Metformin** mildly inhibits Complex I (or mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase) and can blunt training-induced gains in mitochondrial respiration and VO2max in older adults (Konopka et al., 2019).
- **Cyanide and carbon monoxide** block Complex IV; tissues can't use oxygen even if delivered.
- **Mitochondrial uncouplers** such as 2,4-dinitrophenol dissipate the proton gradient as heat, causing hyperthermia; toxicity is severe.
- High-dose antioxidants may blunt adaptive signaling from reactive oxygen species (Ristow et al., 2009), though results vary.

**Open questions.** How much does mitochondrial efficiency (P/O) vary between people and with training? Dietary nitrate's reported improvement in O2 cost (Larsen et al., 2011) has inconsistent replication. Mitochondrial protein turnover, mitophagy (PINK1/Parkin) and contact sites with the sarcoplasmic reticulum are active areas. Sex differences and age-related decline in mitochondrial quality remain unclear: how much is inactivity versus intrinsic aging?

keyPoints: Oxidative phosphorylation makes most ATP in efforts lasting longer than about 2 minutes
Fuels become acetyl-CoA, which feeds the Krebs cycle to produce NADH and FADH2
The electron transport chain pumps protons; oxygen is the final electron acceptor
ATP synthase uses the proton gradient to make about 30-32 ATP per glucose
ADP and calcium from contraction switch on mitochondrial respiration
Training builds more mitochondria via PGC-1alpha signaling

test.q: Where in muscle cells does oxidative phosphorylation take place?
test.explain: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase sit in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis, by contrast, happens in the cytoplasm.

test.q: What is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain?
test.explain: Oxygen accepts electrons at Complex IV and combines with protons to form water.

test.q: Roughly how many ATP come from fully oxidizing one glucose molecule?
test.explain: Full oxidation yields about 30-32 ATP. Glycolysis alone yields only 2.

test.q: Which molecule carries carbon from both glucose and fat into the Krebs cycle?
test.explain: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and beta-oxidation both produce acetyl-CoA, which enters the TCA cycle.

test.q: According to the chemiosmotic theory, what directly drives ATP synthase?
choices: Release of calcium from the reticulum
Flow of protons back across the membrane
test.explain: The proton gradient built by the chain flows back through ATP synthase, rotating it to make ATP.

test.q: Which enzyme lets long-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria?
test.explain: CPT-1 controls entry of long-chain fatty acids for beta-oxidation. Pyruvate dehydrogenase handles pyruvate, not fatty acids.

test.q: What chiefly accelerates mitochondrial respiration when contraction starts?
choices: Falling oxygen levels in the blood
test.explain: ATP use raises ADP (respiratory control), while calcium activates PDH and TCA dehydrogenases.

test.q: Compared with glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation provides ATP:
test.explain: OXPHOS has a lower maximal rate but a much higher yield, so it dominates long efforts.

test.q: Which complex feeds electrons into the chain without pumping protons?
test.explain: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) passes FADH2-derived electrons to ubiquinone but pumps no protons, which is why FADH2 yields less ATP.

test.q: Name the coactivator protein that acts as a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis with training.
test.explain: AMPK, CaMKII and p38 signals converge on PGC-1α, which drives new mitochondria.

test.q: The Krebs cycle is also called the citric ___ cycle.
test.explain: It is the citric acid (TCA) cycle.

test.q: What rotating enzyme makes ATP using the proton gradient?
test.explain: ATP synthase (Complex V) couples proton flow to ATP synthesis.

kidTest.q: What are the tiny power plants in muscles called?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria make most of the energy for long activities.

kidTest.q: What do these power plants need from the air you breathe?
kidTest.explain: They use oxygen to burn food for energy.

kidTest.q: This kind of energy is best for which activity?
kidTest.explain: It is slow but lasts a long time, perfect for long activities.

kidTest.q: What happens to your muscles if you train a lot?
kidTest.explain: Training makes muscles grow more mitochondria.

kidTest.q: What are the energy coins your muscles spend called? (A _ _)
kidTest.explain: ATP is the energy coin of cells.

advancedTest.q: Apparent Km for ADP is far higher in permeabilized slow-twitch fibers than in isolated mitochondria. The best interpretation is:
choices: Isolation strips creatine kinase from the mitochondria
ATP synthase in fibers carries a lower affinity mutation
Diffusion restriction makes creatine shuttle signaling important
Slow fibers rely on glycolysis instead of mitochondria
advancedTest.explain: Restricted ADP access via VDAC/tubulin means the MtCK-PCr shuttle carries much of the energy signal in intact fibers.

advancedTest.q: A patient has low peak VO2 and an unusually high venous O2 saturation during exercise. This most suggests:
choices: Impaired muscle O2 use from an OXPHOS defect
advancedTest.explain: Oxygen arrives but is not extracted, giving a narrow a-vO2 difference typical of mitochondrial myopathy; deconditioning usually preserves extraction.

advancedTest.q: VO2 can rise many-fold with only small changes in ADP. Which idea best explains this?
choices: Parallel activation of multiple OXPHOS steps
Respiration is mainly set by oxygen tension
Proton leak rises sharply during exercise
Glycolysis supplies extra NADH to the chain
advancedTest.explain: Korzeniewski's each-step activation proposes that Ca2+ and other signals co-activate many complexes, so flux rises without large metabolite shifts.

advancedTest.q: PGC-1α knockout mice still show training adaptations. What does this imply?
choices: Training adaptations come mainly from the heart
PGC-1α blocks biogenesis in normal animals
Mitochondrial biogenesis does not happen in mice
Redundant pathways can drive mitochondrial adaptation
advancedTest.explain: Adaptation without PGC-1α shows other signaling routes can compensate, so it is important but not essential.

lessons.title: Fat vs Carbohydrate: The Crossover Concept

levels.kid:
Your muscles are like a car that can use two kinds of fuel. One fuel is **fat**. Your body has a huge tank of it, but it burns slowly. The other fuel is **sugar**, stored in your muscles and liver. It burns fast, but the tank is small.

When you walk, your muscles mostly use fat. Slow and steady works fine.

When you sprint or race up a hill, your muscles need energy fast. So they switch to burning more sugar.

The point where sugar becomes the main fuel is called the **crossover**.

If you run for a very long time, the sugar tank can get low. Then you feel super tired. Runners call it "hitting the wall."
levels.hs:
Skeletal muscle makes ATP mainly from two fuels: **carbohydrate** (glucose from the blood and **glycogen**, the stored form of glucose in muscle and liver) and **fat** (fatty acids from fat tissue and from fat droplets inside muscle).

The two fuels have different strengths:
- Fat stores are enormous. Even a lean person carries enough fat to fuel days of walking. But fat is broken down and burned relatively slowly, and it needs more oxygen per ATP.
- Carbohydrate stores are small, enough for roughly 90 to 120 minutes of hard exercise. But carbohydrate can be burned quickly, and it yields more ATP per unit of oxygen.

The **crossover concept**, proposed by George Brooks and Jacques Mercier in 1994, describes how fuel use shifts with exercise intensity. At rest and during easy exercise, fat supplies most of the energy. As intensity rises, carbohydrate contributes a larger share. The **crossover point** is the intensity where carbohydrate becomes the main fuel.

Scientists estimate the fuel mix with the **respiratory exchange ratio (RER)**, the ratio of CO2 breathed out to O2 taken in. An RER near 0.7 means mostly fat. An RER near 1.0 means mostly carbohydrate.

A real example: marathoners who run low on glycogen "hit the wall" around mile 20. Fat alone cannot supply energy fast enough to hold race pace, so they slow down.
levels.college:
**The crossover concept** (Brooks & Mercier, 1994) states that the relative contribution of carbohydrate (CHO) to energy supply rises with exercise intensity, while fat's relative contribution falls. The **crossover point** is the power output beyond which CHO supplies more energy than lipid. In untrained people it often falls around 40-50% of VO2max, and training shifts it to higher intensities.

**Measuring the mix.** Indirect calorimetry gives RER (VCO2/VO2). Complete oxidation of glucose yields an RQ of 1.0 (6 O2 in, 6 CO2 out). A typical fatty acid such as palmitate yields about 0.70 (23 O2 in, 16 CO2 out). Stable-isotope tracers separate plasma glucose, muscle glycogen, plasma free fatty acids (FFA) and intramuscular triglyceride (IMTG).

**Why CHO takes over as intensity rises:**
- Recruitment of more type II fibers, which are more glycolytic.
- Rising **adrenaline** speeds glycogen breakdown through phosphorylase activation, and higher Ca2+ adds to the effect.
- Greater glycolytic flux limits fat entry into mitochondria (see below).
- CHO yields about 5.0 kcal per liter of O2, versus about 4.7 for fat, so it is more oxygen-efficient when O2 delivery is limiting.

**Fat oxidation peaks, then falls.** Absolute fat oxidation rises from rest to moderate intensity (**Fatmax**, often ~45-65% VO2max), then declines. Romijn and colleagues (1993) showed plasma FFA uptake falling at 85% VO2max, while muscle glycogen became the dominant fuel.

**Duration matters too.** During prolonged steady exercise, glycogen falls and fat use gradually rises.

**Diet and training shift the curve.** Endurance training increases mitochondrial density and fat-oxidation enzymes and spares glycogen. High-CHO diets raise glycogen and RER. Fasting and high-fat diets lower RER.
levels.phd:
Fuel selection reflects competition at several control points rather than a single switch.

**Randle cycle (1963).** Raised FFA oxidation increases acetyl-CoA/CoA and NADH/NAD+. This inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and raises citrate, which inhibits phosphofructokinase (PFK) and slows glucose uptake. The cycle explains fat suppressing CHO use at rest. During exercise, however, Ca2+ and adrenaline override it, and the reverse direction dominates.

**Reverse Randle: CHO limits fat oxidation.** As glycolytic flux rises, three mechanisms limit fat use:
- **Malonyl-CoA**, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, inhibits **CPT1**, the gate for long-chain fatty acid entry into mitochondria. In human muscle, however, malonyl-CoA changes during exercise are small, so this cannot be the whole story.
- **Carnitine sequestration** is now emphasized (van Loon 2001). At high PDH flux, excess acetyl-CoA is buffered as acetylcarnitine, depleting free carnitine and limiting CPT1 substrate.
- Falling pH at high intensity directly inhibits CPT1.

Medium-chain fatty acids bypass CPT1, and their oxidation is less impaired at high intensity. This supports a CPT1-level restriction.

**Supply limits.** At high intensity, adipose blood flow falls and FFA can be re-esterified within the tissue, so plasma FFA availability drops. Albumin-bound FFA delivery and the transporter CD36 also constrain uptake. IMTG lipolysis via ATGL and HSL contributes, especially in trained muscle.

**PDH activation** by Ca2+, pyruvate and reduced PDK activity commits pyruvate to oxidation. Lactate turnover and its re-oxidation link this to Brooks' shuttle framework.

**Quantitative nuance.** Maximal fat oxidation (MFO) varies widely between individuals (roughly 0.2-1.0 g/min in large datasets) and depends on sex, training, diet and protocol. Women oxidize relatively more fat at a given relative intensity, partly through estrogen. RER can be confounded by hyperventilation and by bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid above threshold, which inflates VCO2. Protein oxidation, usually under 5-10% of energy, is ignored in non-protein RQ calculations.
levels.expert:
The crossover concept has practical and clinical uses well beyond the textbook graph.

**Diet manipulation and performance.** Keto-adaptation (high-fat, low-CHO) can raise peak fat oxidation to over 1.5 g/min (FASTER study, Volek 2016). Burke's Supernova trials (2017, 2020) in elite race walkers, however, found that adaptation impaired performance despite better fat use. It reduced exercise economy, raising O2 cost at race pace, and impaired PDH activity even after CHO was restored. This is the oxygen-efficiency argument made concrete: at high intensity, O2 per ATP matters. "Train low, compete high" periodization (sleep-low, fasted sessions) tries to gain mitochondrial signaling through AMPK and PGC-1alpha without sacrificing race-day CHO availability. Its performance benefits remain mixed.

**Exogenous CHO.** Intestinal SGLT1 saturates at about 1 g/min glucose oxidation. Glucose-fructose mixtures recruit GLUT5 and allow higher total exogenous oxidation. Carbohydrate mouth-rinse effects suggest central, not just metabolic, contributions in shorter events.

**Clinical relevance.**
- **Metabolic inflexibility** (Kelley & Mandarino) is the impaired ability to switch between fuels, seen in obesity and type 2 diabetes. It shows up as a blunted fall in RER with fasting and a blunted rise with insulin.
- **Fatty acid oxidation disorders** (CPT2 deficiency, VLCAD deficiency) cause exertional rhabdomyolysis during prolonged or fasted exercise, when fat dependence peaks.
- **McArdle disease** (myophosphorylase deficiency) produces a "second wind" as FFA delivery rises after about 8-10 minutes. It is a natural experiment in glycogen-independent fuel supply.
- Beta-blockade blunts lipolysis and glycogenolysis and alters the fuel mix.

**Pitfalls.** Fatmax prescription for weight loss overstates the point: total energy expenditure, not fuel source during the session, drives fat loss. Lab RER is sensitive to the previous meal, caffeine and protocol stage length.

**Open questions.** How much does IMTG really contribute, given its contested measurement by biopsy versus MRS? What explains the large individual variation in Fatmax? Are the PDH impairments after keto-adaptation reversible?

keyPoints: Fat stores are huge but slow; carbohydrate stores are small but fast and oxygen-efficient
Crossover concept: carbohydrate's share of energy rises with exercise intensity
RER near 0.7 means mostly fat; near 1.0 means mostly carbohydrate
Fat oxidation peaks at moderate intensity (Fatmax), then falls
CPT1 gating, carnitine sequestration and falling FFA supply limit fat use at high intensity
Training shifts the crossover point to higher intensities and spares glycogen

test.q: According to the crossover concept, what happens as exercise intensity rises?
choices: Protein becomes the main fuel source
The fuel mix stays roughly constant
Fat supplies a growing share of energy
test.explain: As intensity rises, carbohydrate's relative contribution increases and fat's falls. Protein usually supplies less than 5-10% of energy.

test.q: An RER of about 0.70 indicates the body is mainly oxidizing:
test.explain: Fatty acid oxidation gives an RQ near 0.70, while carbohydrate gives 1.0.

test.q: Why does carbohydrate become favored when oxygen delivery limits performance?
choices: It produces no carbon dioxide when burned
Its stores are larger than fat stores
It needs no mitochondria to be oxidized
It yields more ATP per liter of oxygen
test.explain: Carbohydrate yields about 5.0 kcal per liter of O2 versus about 4.7 for fat. Its stores are actually much smaller than fat stores.

test.q: What happens to absolute fat oxidation from rest to very high intensity?
choices: It rises steadily the whole way
It falls steadily from rest onward
It rises to a peak, then declines
test.explain: Fat oxidation peaks at moderate intensity (Fatmax), then declines as carbohydrate takes over.

test.q: How does endurance training affect the crossover point?
choices: It has no measurable effect on it
It shifts it to higher intensities
It shifts it to lower intensities
test.explain: More mitochondria and fat-oxidation enzymes let trained muscle rely on fat at higher intensities, sparing glycogen.

test.q: Which hormone rises with intensity and speeds glycogen breakdown?
test.explain: Adrenaline activates phosphorylase, increasing glycogenolysis. Insulin promotes storage instead.

test.q: Which enzyme acts as the gate for long-chain fatty acids entering mitochondria?
test.explain: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1) controls long-chain fatty acid entry and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA and low pH.

test.q: Why do marathoners 'hit the wall' late in a race?
choices: Muscle protein becomes the main fuel
Their fat stores have run out
test.explain: When glycogen runs low, fat alone cannot supply ATP fast enough to hold race pace. Fat stores are nowhere near exhausted.

test.q: During prolonged steady exercise at the same intensity, the fuel mix gradually:
test.explain: As glycogen falls over time, fat oxidation gradually rises.

test.q: What is the name of the exercise intensity at which absolute fat oxidation peaks?
test.explain: Fatmax is often around 45-65% VO2max but varies widely between people.

test.q: The stored form of glucose in muscle and liver is called ___.
test.explain: Glycogen stores are small, enough for roughly 90-120 minutes of hard exercise.

test.q: The CO2-to-O2 measure used to estimate fuel mix is the ___ exchange ratio.
test.explain: The respiratory exchange ratio (RER) = VCO2/VO2, measured by indirect calorimetry.

kidTest.q: Which fuel do muscles mostly use when you walk slowly?
kidTest.explain: Easy exercise mostly burns fat, slow and steady.

kidTest.q: What do muscles burn more of when you sprint?
kidTest.explain: Sugar burns fast, so it gives quick energy for sprinting.

kidTest.q: Which fuel tank is the biggest in your body?
kidTest.explain: Fat stores are huge, but they burn slowly.

kidTest.q: What do runners call running low on sugar?
kidTest.explain: When the sugar tank gets low, runners feel very tired and call it hitting the wall.

kidTest.q: The point where sugar becomes the main fuel is called the c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: It's where the muscles cross over from mostly fat to mostly sugar.

advancedTest.q: Medium-chain fatty acid oxidation is relatively preserved at high intensity while long-chain oxidation falls. This best supports:
choices: Depletion of intramuscular triglyceride during the first minutes
Saturation of intestinal SGLT1 transport by long-chain fats
A limit on fat use at the level of mitochondrial CPT1 entry
A failure of adipose lipolysis caused by rising insulin levels
advancedTest.explain: Medium-chain fatty acids bypass CPT1, so their preservation points to restriction at CPT1, via carnitine sequestration and low pH.

advancedTest.q: Above the lactate threshold, measured RER can exceed 1.0. The most likely reason is:
choices: Protein oxidation becomes the dominant energy source
Fat oxidation stops and glucose produces extra oxygen
Bicarbonate buffering of acid adds non-metabolic CO2
Muscle begins to make fat from glucose during exercise
advancedTest.explain: Buffering lactic acid with bicarbonate releases extra CO2, and hyperventilation inflates VCO2, so RER no longer reflects substrate oxidation alone.

advancedTest.q: Keto-adapted elite walkers oxidized more fat yet raced slower. The best explanation is:
choices: Their fat stores were depleted early in the race
Malonyl-CoA levels rose and blocked glycogen breakdown
Adrenaline release was abolished by the high-fat diet
Higher oxygen cost per ATP and impaired PDH activity
advancedTest.explain: Fat requires more O2 per ATP, reducing economy at race pace, and adaptation impaired PDH even after carbohydrate was restored.

advancedTest.q: A McArdle patient feels better after about 8-10 minutes of exercise. This 'second wind' is best explained by:
choices: Rising fatty acid delivery replacing glycogen-derived fuel
Faster recruitment of glycolytic type II muscle fibers
Delayed recovery of myophosphorylase enzyme activity
Lactate accumulation that directly stimulates CPT1
advancedTest.explain: Without myophosphorylase, glycogen cannot be used. As FFA delivery rises, glycogen-independent fuel supports exercise.

lessons.title: Muscle Fiber Types and Motor Unit Recruitment

levels.kid:
Your muscles are made of tiny threads called **fibers**. Not all fibers are the same!

Some fibers are like tortoises. They are **slow** but they can keep going for a very long time without getting tired. You use them when you walk or stand.

Other fibers are like hares. They are **fast** and super strong, but they get tired quickly. You use them when you sprint or jump.

Your brain sends messages down nerves to tell fibers to work. Each nerve controls a team of fibers. For easy jobs, the brain wakes up the small tortoise teams first. When you need more power, it adds the bigger hare teams too. That way you use just the right amount of muscle.
levels.hs:
Skeletal muscle is built from long cells called **muscle fibers**. Fibers come in main types:
- **Type I (slow-twitch)**: contract slowly, resist fatigue, have many **mitochondria** and lots of **myoglobin** (an oxygen-holding protein that makes them red). They rely mostly on aerobic metabolism.
- **Type IIa (fast oxidative)**: fast and fairly fatigue resistant, a middle type.
- **Type IIx (fast glycolytic)**: fastest and most powerful, but tire quickly because they depend heavily on glycolysis.

A **motor unit** is one motor neuron plus all the fibers it controls. All fibers in a unit are the same type. When the neuron fires, every one of its fibers contracts.

Your nervous system controls force by choosing which units to switch on. This follows the **size principle**, discovered by Elwood Henneman in the 1950s: small motor neurons (controlling slow, type I fibers) are recruited first, and larger ones (controlling type II fibers) are added as more force is needed. The brain can also make units fire faster, called **rate coding**.

Example: marathon runners often have mostly type I fibers in their calf muscles, while elite sprinters have a higher share of type II fibers. Genetics sets much of this mix, but training changes fiber properties.
levels.college:
Muscle fibers are classified mainly by **myosin heavy chain (MHC) isoform**, which sets the rate of ATP hydrolysis by myosin and therefore shortening velocity. In humans the major isoforms are MHC I, IIa and IIx (rodents also express IIb, which adult human limb muscle largely lacks).

**Fiber properties**
- **Type I**: slow myosin ATPase, high mitochondrial and capillary density, high myoglobin, high oxidative enzymes (e.g., citrate synthase, succinate dehydrogenase), small diameter, fatigue resistant.
- **Type IIa**: fast, high oxidative and glycolytic capacity, intermediate fatigue resistance.
- **Type IIx**: fastest, highest glycolytic enzymes and power, lowest oxidative capacity, fatigue quickly.
- **Hybrid fibers** (I/IIa, IIa/IIx) coexpress isoforms and are common, especially during transitions.

Fibers were historically typed by **myosin ATPase histochemistry** at different pH values; today immunohistochemistry and gel electrophoresis of MHC are standard, usually on **needle biopsies** of vastus lateralis.

**Motor units and recruitment**
A motor unit's fibers are homogeneous in type and scattered across the muscle. Muscle force is graded by:
- **Recruitment**: adding units in order of increasing size (Henneman's size principle). Small motor neurons have high input resistance, so a given synaptic current depolarizes them to threshold first.
- **Rate coding**: increasing firing frequency, producing summation and tetanus.

**Link to fuel use**: at low intensity mainly type I units are active, oxidizing fat and glucose. As intensity rises, type II units join, increasing glycogen breakdown and lactate production. This recruitment shift is one reason muscle glycogen in type II fibers depletes later in prolonged or intense exercise, when those units are called on.

**Plasticity**: endurance training shifts IIx toward IIa and raises oxidative capacity in all types; detraining or disuse tends to increase IIx expression. Clear type II to type I conversion in humans is limited.
levels.phd:
Fiber identity is a gene-expression program coordinated by activity-dependent signaling. Tonic, low-frequency firing (typical of slow motor units) produces sustained moderate Ca²⁺ elevations that activate **calcineurin**, dephosphorylating **NFAT** and promoting slow-gene expression (MYH7, myoglobin, slow troponin). Cross-innervation experiments by Buller, Eccles and Eccles (1960) showed that swapping nerves between fast and slow muscles changed their speed, establishing neural control of phenotype. Chronic low-frequency electrical stimulation (Pette) drives a progressive fast-to-slow transition through hybrid states.

Oxidative remodeling depends on **PGC-1α**, induced by AMPK, CaMKII and p38 MAPK; transgenic overexpression of PGC-1α in mice increases slow, oxidative fibers. **Sox6** and the MyomiR network (miR-208b and miR-499, encoded within MYH7 and MYH7b introns) repress fast genes and reinforce the slow program. ACTN3 (α-actinin-3) is expressed in fast fibers; the common R577X null variant is underrepresented among elite sprinters, though it explains little variance in the general population.

**Size principle mechanics.** Henneman's orderly recruitment arises largely from intrinsic motoneuron properties: input resistance scales inversely with soma size and membrane area, so equal synaptic currents produce larger voltage changes in small cells. Persistent inward currents (PICs), mediated by Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels and amplified by serotonergic and noradrenergic neuromodulation from the brainstem, add gain. Recruitment thresholds also correlate with axonal conduction velocity and twitch force. High-density surface EMG decomposition now resolves many concurrently firing units in humans.

**Controversies.** Whether ballistic or eccentric contractions selectively recruit fast units ahead of slow ones is debated; most evidence supports preserved order with compressed thresholds during rapid contractions. Histochemical studies (e.g., Costill, Saltin) found wide ranges of vastus lateralis type I proportion in humans, influenced substantially by heritability, yet biopsy sampling error is large because fiber type varies with depth and region of a muscle.
levels.expert:
**Assessment pitfalls.** A single vastus lateralis biopsy samples a tiny volume of muscle, and fiber proportion varies between sites, so repeated biopsies can differ substantially. Noninvasive proxies are emerging: **carnosine quantification by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy** (carnosine is higher in type II fibers) has been used to estimate fiber typology in athletes, but it remains an indirect estimate. Single-fiber proteomics and single-nucleus RNA-seq now show that fiber types are better viewed as a continuum, with substantial heterogeneity even within an MHC class.

**Fatigue and recruitment.** During sustained submaximal contractions, surface EMG amplitude rises as fatiguing units lose force and new, larger units are recruited to hold output. Interpreting this as "more effort" without decomposition is a common error, since amplitude cancellation and crosstalk distort the signal.

**Clinical neurology.** Reinnervation after denervation, as in motor neuron disease or chronic radiculopathy, produces **fiber-type grouping** on biopsy: surviving axons sprout and convert orphaned fibers to their own type, erasing the normal mosaic. Needle EMG shows large, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials and reduced recruitment (few units firing fast). In ALS, the largest fast-fatigable motor units tend to degenerate earliest, an observation linked to their high metabolic and excitability demands. Corticosteroid myopathy and disuse preferentially cause type II atrophy, while critical illness myopathy involves myosin loss.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** After spinal cord injury, paralyzed muscle shifts toward fast, fatigable phenotypes; functional electrical stimulation recruits motor units in a reversed or nonselective order (large axons have lower electrical thresholds), causing rapid fatigue. Nerve transfer surgery depends on donor axon number and reinnervation timing before motor end-plates degrade.

**Pharmacology.** Exercise mimetics targeting PPARδ (e.g., GW501516) or AMPK (AICAR) increased oxidative fibers and endurance in mice, but toxicity signals halted clinical development, and both are prohibited in sport. Open questions: how much adult human fiber phenotype is truly plastic, and whether myostatin-pathway or ACTN3-informed therapies can preserve type II mass in aging sarcopenia, where type II fibers atrophy preferentially.

keyPoints: Fiber types are defined mainly by myosin heavy chain isoform: I, IIa, IIx
Type I fibers are slow, oxidative and fatigue resistant; IIx are fast, glycolytic and fatigable
A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all the same-type fibers it controls
Henneman's size principle: small motor units are recruited before large ones
Force is graded by recruitment plus rate coding (firing frequency)
Calcineurin-NFAT and PGC-1α link activity patterns to fiber phenotype

test.q: Which property best describes type I muscle fibers?
test.explain: Type I fibers contract slowly but have many mitochondria and myoglobin, so they resist fatigue.

test.q: What is a motor unit?
choices: A bundle of fibers wrapped in connective tissue
A sensory receptor that detects muscle stretch
The contractile segment between two Z discs
One motor neuron and the fibers it controls
test.explain: A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates.

test.q: According to the size principle, which units are recruited first?
choices: Small units with type I fibers
Large units with type IIx fibers
Medium units with type IIa fibers
test.explain: Henneman showed small motor neurons reach threshold first, recruiting slow type I units before larger fast ones.

test.q: Fiber types are classified mainly by which protein's isoform?
test.explain: Myosin heavy chain isoforms (I, IIa, IIx) set ATPase rate and contraction speed.

test.q: Why do type I fibers look red?
test.explain: Myoglobin, an oxygen-binding protein, gives oxidative fibers their red color.

test.q: Increasing the firing frequency of active motor units to raise force is called:
test.explain: Rate coding raises force by firing units faster; recruitment adds new units.

test.q: Which change is most typical after endurance training in humans?
choices: Type I fibers convert to IIx
test.explain: Endurance training shifts IIx toward IIa and boosts oxidative capacity; full conversion to type I is limited.

test.q: As exercise intensity rises, recruitment of type II units mainly increases use of:
test.explain: Type II fibers rely heavily on glycolysis, so their recruitment raises glycogen breakdown and lactate.

test.q: Which fiber type produces the most power but tires fastest?
test.explain: Type IIx fibers have the fastest myosin and high glycolytic capacity but low oxidative capacity.

test.q: The size principle of orderly recruitment is named after Elwood ___.
test.explain: Henneman described recruitment from small to large motor neurons in the 1950s.

test.q: Which muscle is usually sampled by needle biopsy to determine fiber type in humans?
test.explain: The vastus lateralis of the thigh is the standard biopsy site.

test.q: Fibers that express two myosin isoforms at once are called ___ fibers.
test.explain: Hybrid fibers such as IIa/IIx coexpress isoforms, often during transitions.

kidTest.q: Which fibers can keep working for a long time?
kidTest.explain: Slow fibers are like tortoises: they keep going without tiring.

kidTest.q: Which fibers help most when you sprint?
kidTest.explain: Fast fibers are strong and quick, like hares.

kidTest.q: What tells muscle fibers when to work?
kidTest.explain: The brain sends messages down nerves to the fibers.

kidTest.q: For an easy job, which teams does the brain use first?
kidTest.explain: Small slow teams start first; bigger fast teams join when more power is needed.

kidTest.q: Muscles are made of tiny threads called f _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Muscle fibers are the tiny threads that pull to make you move.

advancedTest.q: Why are small motor neurons recruited before large ones given equal synaptic input?
choices: Larger numbers of synapses form on their dendrites
Higher input resistance produces a larger depolarization
Faster axons deliver the signal to fibers earlier
Lower thresholds result from heavy myelination
advancedTest.explain: By Ohm's law, the same current across higher input resistance yields a bigger voltage change, reaching threshold first.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows large patches of same-type fibers instead of a mosaic. This most suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Sprouting surviving axons convert orphaned fibers to their own type, producing fiber-type grouping.

advancedTest.q: Functional electrical stimulation after spinal cord injury causes rapid fatigue mainly because:
choices: Large axons have lower electrical thresholds
Slow units lose their mitochondria within minutes
Stimulation selectively spares large fast units
advancedTest.explain: External current activates large axons readily, reversing or scrambling physiological order and engaging fatigable units.

advancedTest.q: Surface EMG amplitude rises during a sustained submaximal hold. Which inference is best supported?
choices: Fewer motor units are firing as the hold continues
Fast units have been converted to slow phenotypes
Myosin ATPase activity has increased in type I fibers
Additional units are recruited to offset fatigued ones
advancedTest.explain: As active units lose force, larger units are recruited to maintain output, though amplitude cancellation complicates interpretation.
